notable.report: The 1RAR advance guard arrived at Bien Hoa. Over the next few days other elements of 1RAR arrived gradually bringing the battalion to full strength. Beginning on 6 June, 1RAR NCOs and  soldiers went on ambush and other TAOR patrols with 2/503 US battalion to familiarise with operations in Vietnam. Meanwhile, drafts of 1RAR personnel continued to arrive by air and aboard HMAS Sydney. By 11 June, officers and men of 1RAR were sending out their own patrols into the TAOR but despite the patrolling effort each patrol returned with nothing to report. On 15 June, the Prince of Wales Light Horse, with 10 M113 APCs and one officer and 28 men came under command of 1RAR. 1RAR's first shot in anger appears to have been fired by the mortar platoon on 25 June when the platoon fired on a suspected enemy village. The battalion's first sighting of the enemy came on 26 June when two VC camps were found and five VC were seen but escaped before a cordon could be put in place. 26 June also brought the battalion's first casualties when the accidental discharge of an M26 grenade caused two KIA, one DOW and 7 WIA. One American was KIA and two WIA. The first casualty resulting from enemy action appears to have been LT R. Hill, PWLH, who was wounded in the stomach by harrassing fire on 28 June.
notable.archivalSource: AWM95, item 7/1/26, 1 Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, Narrative and Annexes 30 Apr-30 Jun 1965, pp. 5-15.

units: 1 APC Troop, Prince of Wales Light Horse Regiment

notable.report: 1 RAR secured the road Vo Dat/Chanh Duc and later, carried out preparatory moves for an assault on Vo Xu village (YT815380) on 26 Nov 65. At 0650 hours on the morning of 26 November, C Company, mounted in 1 APC troop, moved off to carry out a frontal assault down the road Chanh Duc/Vo Xu on the village of Vo Xu. A Company was to move north west of the village to provide support if necessary. B and D companies were to give diversionary fire from positions at the south west corner of the village. At 0807 hours, C Company received light fire on entering Vo Xu village but quickly managed to secure the south west of the village (which was the objective). Two VC were understood to have escaped through tunnels as the leading elements of C Company advanced.
notable.archivalSource: AWM95, item 7/1/39, 1 Battalion Royal Australian Regiment, Narrative, Annexes, 1-30 Nov 1965, p. 22-23.

notable.report: 1 RAR moved from Chanh Duc village to nearby Vo Xu village. Little trouble was encountered moving into the village. 52 VC were catured and 7b VC rallied to battalion sub-units. During the afternoon the remainder of Vo Xu village was cleared. Machinegun fire was encountered near the eastern end of the village. Two soldiers were wounded. One, Cpl R.H. Hillier, later died of his wounds. Pte D. Ryder suffered a shrapnel wound. 2LT Bolitho reported that his 4 Platoon was part of a B Company cordon around Vo Xu village. As the sweep neared the south east corner of the village the right section of Bolitho's platoon received fire from across the La Nga river. The enemy strength was estimated to be about platoon minus. They were  armed with 2 MGs (possibly BARs), rifles and light calibre automatic weapons. Bolitho thought the enemy were attempting to support the escapee of other VC by boat across the river. Four boates were tied up on the bank of the river. Bolitho's platoon returned fire with two M60s and M79 fire also engaging the enemy position with mortar and artillery fire. Helicopter support was also used. Bolitho estimated that 4 enemy had been KIA but his platoon did not recover any bodies.
notable.archivalSource: AWM95, item 7/1/39, 1 Battalion Royal Australian Regiment, Narrative, Annexes, 1-30 Nov 1965, p. 25. 2LT Bolitho's After Action Report is at AWM95, item 7/1/46, 1 Battalion Royal Australian Regiment, Annex Material, 1-30 Nov 1965, p. 38.

units: B Company, 1 Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment
notable.report: Engineers brought forward a Mighty Mite team to blow smoke and CS gas into the tunnels found by B Company and other 1RAR elements on previous days. It was hoped that the smoke forced into the tunnels would reveal where other entrances were located. The CS gas would be used to deny the tunnels to enemy occupation. During an inspection of one of the tunnel entrances, Cpl Bowtell (RAE) was asphixiated by a combination of CS gas and lack of oxygen. He was located in a vertical shaft between the first and second levels of tunnels. In his struggles he had dislodged his respirator and when rescue parties eventually reached him, he was found to be dead. Two other soldiers were badly affected during their attempts to reach Cpl Bowtell and were dusted off. Other important documents were found in the tunnel system including an excellently presented propaganda book of photographs prepared by the Saigon Cholon Gia Dinh Committee. Other caches  were discovered within the B Company perimeter. These included food, documents, and  medical stores. One cache was found in a tunnel entrance with a sophisticated hinged wooden trap door entry. From the trap door, wires led to two booby traps. The booby traps were grenades in plastic bags. Both wires had been pulled but had broken because the grenade pins had been left splayed.
notable.archivalSource: Major Ian McFarlane's Operational Analysis is at AWM95, item 7/1/56, 1 Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, Annexes, 1-31 Jan 1966, p. 12-19.

units: 12 Platoon, D Company, 1 Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment
notable.report: 12 Platoon was clearing the company area in preparation for a battalion harbour. As the platoon swept the area it was ambushed by a VC patrol. Two grenades were detonated by the VC who then opened fire with automatic weapons, wounding one 12 platoon soldier. The right forward section implemented a contact drill and received another two  grenades and further automatic and rifle fire from the VC ambush position. A further three 12 platoon soldiers were wounded. 12 Platoon returned fire. The rear section swept to the east in extended line. The platoon commander moved forward to the lead section and was wounded. Two medics went forward to assist the wounded but both were killed while  another soldier was wounded. Meanwhile, the section sweeping to the east became pinned down by enemy automatic fire and grenades from well constructed  bunkers. Another 12 platoon soldier was wounded. The company support section  did a right flank attack and met no opposition. After the contact was over the dead and wounded were evacuated. Enemy strength was estimated at 4 to 7 men, probably about a section. The incident had take 1 hour and 20 minutes. Later, engineers recovered clothing, rice, weapons, ammunition and grenades from the bunkers. Weapons recovered were 4 bolt action Russian made rifles. Own casualties were 2 killed and 6 wounded. The ambush had been set up to cover an area of open country that the platoon had walked into. Lessons identified by the platoon commander, Sgt J.W. Carnes, were to avoid open areas and keep medics out of the action until safe to send them forward.
notable.archivalSource: Sgt Carnes' After Action Report is at AWM95, item 7/1/56, 1 Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, Annexes, 1-31 Jan 1966, p. 44-45.

notable.report:
Tanks and infantry from Coral attacked a number of bunker systems in the vicinity of FSPB Coral.

D Coy with tank support returns to the site of B Coy contact of 25 May. An air strike was delivered at  1050hrs. At 1140hrs, D coy with tanks moved into the same area and soon came under RPG, MG and AK47 fire from a well constructed bunker system to hold a coy. The infantry protected the tanks while the latter cleared the jungle with cannister, and blew up or crushed bunkers. Supported by tanks 10 pl kill 3 en.  Contact was halted at  1315hrs but resumed at 1420hrs (GRXT930313) 12 pl joined 10 pl and 14 bunkers were destroyed and at least 3 more en killed. En fired RPG-2 at tanks but had no effect. Aust Inf used flame throwers.

At 1520hrs the action was broken off because of fading light. The force withdrew behind accurate arty and mortar fire. 14 bunkers were destroyed for no loss. Enemy had 7 definitely killed and an unknown number crushed in bunkers. Bunker total was probably closer to 18 but enemy were buried and crushed in their bunkers by tanks. (See Contact Rept from Tanks)

Noted in Combined Arms Data Base

C coy 1 RAR was conducting a Recce in force and contacted 3 enemy. The coy came under heavy Mortar, MG, RPD and RPG fire from a bunker system, and became pinned down.  LFT and artillery supported C coy but were not particularly effective because of the close range of most contacts (10-15m). They did silence enemy mortars. Attempts by 1 Tp APCs to push through the jungle did not succeed. At 1000hrs 2 tanks arrived from FSPB Coral, and an assault was launched on the camp. 8 bunkers were destroyed. 1 APC was hit by an RPG while evacuating wounded. At 1155hrs C coy broke contact to allow airstrikes on the bunkers. Enemy lost 24 killed with another 8 probably killed.  Another 13 NVA were possibly killed by air and arty. Australians lost 1 killed 7 wounded. Wounds were 1 with gunshot to left leg, 1 with frag wd to upper left arm, 1 with gunshot wds to abdomen and left leg, 1 with frag wd to left thigh, 1 with frag wd to right leg, 1 with frag wd to upper left arm, 1 with gunshot wds to right arm and both legs and shrapnel wd to base of skull.  

C Coy returned to battle site 2 June and discovered 5 en bodies and the stench of many more buried by bomb blasts and arty shells. (AWM95 7-1-80.pdf pg12)
